verdict.reasoning: Patient reports upper lip swelling and difficulty breathing after prawn soup: "there is like a swelling on my, on my upper lip" and later "I feel like I can't breathe that well right now" following ingestion of prawn soup.

Timing of prawn soup: Doctor asks, "So when did you have the prawn soup?" Patient: "That was, that must have been just after work, so maybe like around seven." Doctor confirms: "OK, around seven o'clock."

Onset and location: Patient says lip felt weird "in the corner sort of on the left first" and later: "it must have been like, must have been like, I don't know half an hour maybe" when asked how long it took for swelling to develop. She adds "there is like a swelling on my, on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger."
Doctor asks about throat closing; patient responds: "Yeah actually, I, I feel like I can't breathe that well right now." This supports difficulty breathing and concern about throat involvement.

Doctor: "do you feel like, like your chest is tight?" Patient: "And I don't know if it's the chest it just generally feels a little difficult, but yeah it might be, I'm not sure." This reflects uncertainty about chest tightness.
Patient states during the call: "Ohh, I feel a little dizzy right now to be honest, ohh."
Patient: "I generally have asthma so, I took I, I take, ohh what's it called? Salbutamol inhalers?" and "I generally have asthma."
Patient: "I have a peanut allergy as well, like always had it."

Patient describes prior episode: "I remember that after like having that very late. I've woke up the next morning quite swollen up and had also I, felt really bad and quite difficult breathing, but I don't know what it was I had it was like a curry or something I think." She had been at a late-night Chinese place about a year ago.

Regarding childhood reaction: Doctor asks about hospital/severe reaction; Patient: "When I was a kid I think I remember my mom told me about it" and later "Yeah is that well I was like six or something." Doctor: "your mum ever said that you had to go to hospital because you had an severe allergic reaction?" Patient answers affirmatively. Injection type is unknown, consistent with "injection unknown."
Patient: "I generally have asthma so, I took I, I take, ohh what's it called? Salbutamol inhalers?... Yeah, so I do take that regularly but I've always taken it."
Doctor: "And any other inhalers? Is it just the Salbutamol that you use? Any other brown inhalers?" Patient: "Ohh I, no I don't think so, no."

On antihistamines: Doctor asks if she uses any; Patient: "Hmm, no. I, I got no I do sometimes but I don't know which ones, but I have a peanut allergy as well... I, think I do get antihistamines for that but I'm not sure which ones."
Explicitly stated: "I have a peanut allergy as well, like always had it."

Reaction followed prawn soup: Patient: "I ordered a prawn soup" and then developed lip swelling and breathing difficulty; Doctor interprets as likely anaphylactic reaction. This supports a suspected reaction after prawn exposure.

Patient initially: "I'm alone at the moment, yeah." Later: "Hey ohh somebody just came, somebody just came yes, I'm not alone any more." and then refers to "Mum, Mum do we have any antihistamines around?" indicating mother arrived during the call.

Doctor: "It sounds like you could be going into what we say an a, an anaphylactic reaction." History includes prawn ingestion, upper lip swelling (angioedema), difficulty breathing, throat symptoms queried, and dizziness: "I feel like I can't breathe that well right now" and "I feel a little dizzy right now" with onset about half an hour after eating and worsening: "it's kind of getting bigger it feels like it's getting worse."

Asthma management: patient uses only Salbutamol inhaler and denies other/brown inhalers: "I generally have asthma"; "Salbutamol inhalers"; "any other brown inhalers?" – "no I don't think so." This is consistent with SABA-only management.

Peanut allergy with severe childhood reaction: supported by peanut allergy statement and discussion of hospital/severe reaction with injection in childhood. No adrenaline auto-injector (AAI) is mentioned anywhere, so noting that none is documented is consistent with the transcript.

Doctor: "I think we need to call an ambulance" and later instructs: "Mum, if you can call the uh nine nine , nine nine nine yeah, and say that your there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction and they need to come straight away."

Doctor: "is there any, anyone with you at the moment or are you alone?" then after someone arrives: "make sure that person's with you till the ambulance comes, yeah. Uh and because we are worried about an anaphylactic reaction so you need go straight away." This implies staying with another person until EMS and going to hospital.

Doctor: "Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around, in the interim, while we're waiting." and later: "All right, so straight away take the antihistamines in the meantime all right."

Doctor: "And after you come out from the hospital do give us a ring back we might need to sort you out, um, with your injections and things like that OK?" This refers to arranging future emergency allergy treatment devices.
